question: How should trained ML models be documented so users can judge performance across groups and conditions and avoid unsuited uses?
hypothesis: Short standardized documents with disaggregated, intersectional evaluation and intended-use statements will increase transparency and reduce harmful deployment.
contributions: A framework called model cards: short documents accompanying released models
Two worked example cards: a smiling classifier on CelebA and Perspective API TOXICITY v1 and v5

results.claim: Model cards are proposed as short records accompanying released models.
results.setup: Proposal for any trained ML model, focused on human-centered CV and NLP models
results.quote: we propose that released machine learning models be accompanied by short (one to two page) records we call model cards

results.claim: In the smiling classifier example, all four error rates at the 0.5 decision threshold fall in the same range.
results.setup: Smiling CNN, CelebA test split, 0.5 threshold, 95% bootstrap CIs, gender and age groups
results.quote: All metrics reported at the .5 decision threshold, where all error types (FPR, FNR, FDR, FOR) are within the same range (0.04 - 0.14).
results.note: Per-group numbers are in a figure image, not in the text

results.claim: In the smiling example, false discovery rate on older men is much higher than for other groups, and men overall have a higher false negative rate.
results.setup: CelebA smiling classifier, gender by age groups
results.quote: the false discovery rate on older men is much higher than that for other groups

results.claim: TOXICITY v1 scored poorly for terms such as lesbian, gay, homosexual; v5 has more equitable performance after bias mitigation.
results.setup: Perspective API TOXICITY v1 vs v5, synthetic Identity Phrase Templates test set (Dixon et al. 2018), intersectional version
results.quote: TOXICITY v. 1 has low performance for several terms, especially “lesbian”, “gay”, and “homosexual”.
results.note: Numeric values only in Figure 3 image

results.claim: The authors concede model cards are unlikely to be standardized enough to prevent misleading representations and depend on the creator's integrity.
results.quote: the usefulness and accuracy of a model card relies on the integrity of the creator(s) of the card itself

limits: No empirical test of whether cards change stakeholder behavior; future work to study how stakeholders interpret cards
Section list is explicitly not complete or exhaustive
Evaluation datasets suitable for disaggregated evaluation are not yet common
Smiling example lacks race and skin type and treats gender as binary; toxicity synthetic test set is small and not comprehensive
Training data section may be impossible for proprietary data
Cards are one transparency tool among many (audits, adversarial testing, user feedback)
practices: Release models with a one-to-two-page model card (Section 1).
Report quantitative results disaggregated by unitary and intersectional groups, with confidence intervals where possible (Sections 4.7, 4.4.3).
State intended uses, intended users and out-of-scope uses (Section 4.2).
List all confusion-matrix error rates and say which were prioritized and why (Section 4.4.1).
State decision thresholds and why chosen; offer a threshold slider in digital cards (Section 4.4).
Describe how variability is computed, e.g. average of 5 runs, 10-fold cross-validation (Section 4.4).
Use evaluation data that is publicly available and covers typical and challenging cases; consider synthetic data for uncovered groups (Section 4.5).
Where training data cannot be shared, give basic distributions over groups (Section 4.6).
Use self-identified or clearly perceived-labelled group attributes (Section 2).
Update the card with each new model release, as v1 vs v5 shows (Section 5.2).

terms.definition: short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions
Quantitative analyses should be disaggregated, that is, broken down by the chosen factors.
looking at two or more characteristics such as gender and age simultaneously
measures threshold-agnostic separability of toxic and non-toxic comments for each group, within the context of a background distribution of other groups
